METHODS OF TEST FOR *r- 2007 

PETROLEUM AND ITS PRODUCTS 

[ P : 34 ] 

DETERMINATION OF SULPHUR IN PETROLEUM 
PRODUCTS (LAMP METHOD) 

(Second Revision) 

Third Reprint AUGUST 2006 
( Including Amendment No. 1 ) 

UDC 665.6A7 : 543.845 

Adapted from Joint Publication ASTM Designation D 1266-70 and 
IP Designation 107/73 and ISO Standard No. 2192-1973 

1. SCOPE 

1.1 These methods ( Methods A and B ) cover the determination of total 
sulphur in liquid petroleum products in concentrations above 0002 per- 
cent by mass. A special sulphate analysis procedure is described under 
Method C that permits the determination of sulphur in concentrations as 
low as 5 ppm. Method D describes the determination of sulphur in 
liquefied petroleum gases ( LPG ) and other light hydrocarbon mixtures 
boiling in the same range. 

1.2 The direct burning procedure ( see 7.1 ) is applicable to the analysis 
of such materials as gasoline, kerosine, naphtha, industrial aromatic 
hydrocarbons and other liquids that can be burned completely in a wick 
lamp. The blending procedure ( see 7.2 ) is applicable to the analysis of 
some materials that cannot be burned satisfactorily by the direct 
procedure, such as gas oils, distillate fuel oils, naphthenic acids and alkyl 
phenols. Residual fuel oils, bitumens, tars and other heavy residues can- 
not be analysed by this method. 

® Copyright 1979 

BUREAU OF INDIAN STANDARDS 

MANAK BHAVAN, 9 BAHADUR SHAH 2AFAR MARO 
NEW DELHI 110002 

Gr 7 July 1979 



IS : 1448 [ P : 34 ] - 197ft 



1.3 Phosphorus compounds normally present in commercial gasoline do 
not interfere. A correction is given for the small amount of acid resulting 
from the combustion of the lead anti-knock fluids in gasolines. Appreciable 
concentrations of acid-forming or base-forming elements from other 
sources interfere when the titration procedure is employed since no 
correction is provided in these cases. 

2. OUTLINE OF METHODS 

2.1 The sample is burned in a closed system using a suitable lamp ( see 
Fig. 1 ) and an artificial atmosphere composed of 70 percent carbon 
dioxide and 30 percent oxygen to prevent formation of nitrogen oxides. 
The oxides of sulphur are absorbed and oxidized to sulphuric acid by 
means of hydrogen peroxide solution which is then flushed with air to 
remove dissolved carbon dioxide. Sulphur as sulphate in the absorbent 
is determined acidimetrically by titration with standard sodium hydroxide 
solution ( Method A ) or gravimetrically by precipitation as barium 
sulphate ( Method B ).

2.2 Alternatively, the sample may be burned in sulphur-free air, the 
sulphur as sulphate in the absorbent being determined by precipitation as 
barium sulphate for weighing ( Method B ). 

Note — In the absence of acid-forming or base- forming elements, other than 
sulphur, results by the volumetric and gravimetric finishes described are equivalent 
within the limits of precision of the method. 

2.3 For sulphur contents below 0*002 percent by mass, it is necessary to 
determine the sulphate content in the absorber solution turbidimctrically 
as barium sulphate ( Method C ) . 

3. APPARATUS 

3.1 Combustion Apparatus 

3.1.1 Flask and Burner for Non-aromatic Samples — A lamp of chemically 
resistant glass, consisting of a 25-ml Erlenmeyer flask and a burner that 
conforms to the dimensions shown in Fig. 2 shall be used. The burner 
consists of two concentric glass tubes, the external tube has an arm, 
provided with standard taper glass joints for connection with the flask and 
the chimney. The upper ends of both burner tubes shall be polished, 
having plane surfaces that are in the same horizontal plane. The burner 
shall have a 1-mm opening near its base to allow equilization of pressure 
between the chimney and the flask. When connected with the chimney, 
the lamp shall be held in position by rubber bands or metal springs 
stretched between glass hooks on the flask and chimney. 

Note — The standard flask as shown in Fig. 2 is not suitable for burning highly 
aromatic mixtures without blending ( see 7.2 ). The flask and burner for aromatic 
samples ( Fig. 4) permit burning these samples directly without blending and may 
also be used to burn non-aromatic samples. 

3.1.2 Sample Container and Burner for Liquefied Petroleum Gases — The 
burner is shown in Fig. 3 and the lamp assembly in Fig. 7. The sample 
vessel shall have a capacity of 100 ml and shall be made of stainless steel 
or other corrosion-resistant metal. 

Note — The sample vessel shall be periodically tested at a pressure of 45 mbar 
and shall show no measured deformation at this pressure. 

3.1.3 Flask and Burner for Aromatic Samples — same as described in 3.1.1 
except that: 

a) in dimensions it shall conform to Fig. 4; 

b) with this lamp, a second port with control valve in the burner 
manifold is required; and 

c) the burner shall not have the 1 mm opening.

3.1.4 Chimney — A chimney of chemically resistant glass conforming to 
the dimensions shown in Fig. 2, provided with standard taper glass joints 
for connection with the burner and absorber, shall be used. 

3.2 Absorption Apparatus 

3.2.1 Absorber — An absorber of chemically resistant glass, conforming 
to the dimensions shown in Fig. 2, provided with standard taper glass 
joints for connection with the chimney and spray trap, shall be used. A 
fritted (sintered) disc with average pore diameter from 150 to 200 pim 
shall be sealed in the larger of the two bulbs of the absorber. The fritted 
( sintered ) disc shall be of such a porosity that, when 50 ml of water is 
placed in the absorber and air is passed through at the rate of 30 litres 
per minute in the forward direction, the pressure differential between the 
two sides of the absorber is between 15 and 23 cm of water and the air is 
dispersed uniformly. 

3.2.2 Spray Trap — A spray trap of chemically resistant glass conforming 
to the dimensions shown in Fig. 2, provided with a standard taper glass 
joint for connection with the absorber, shall be used.

Fio. 4 Flask and Burner for Aromatic Samples 

3.3 Cotton Wicking — clean, unused, uniform, twisted white cotton yarn 
of good quality*. For the burner to burn aromatic samples, use long staple, 
fine spun, commercially fine grade. 

3.4 Manifold System — A satisfactory vacuum and combustion atmos- 
phere manifold and supply system for supplying the required carbon 
dioxide-oxygen mixture to the lamp assemblies is shown diagrammatically 
in Fig. 5. It consists of a vacuum manifold with regulating device, valves, 
etc, and a dual manifold ( burner and chimney ) supplying a gas mixture 
of approximately 70 percent {vjv) carbon dioxide and 30 percent ( v/v ) 

•Rug yarn, white, 4-strand ( 2 or 3 mg per cm per strand ) or equivalent material. 



IS: 1448 t P:34]-1S79 

oxygen .at regulated pressures. The gases are supplied from commercial 
cylinders, the pressure of each gas being adjusted to 0*70 ± 0*14 bar by 
means of two single stage regulating valves to ensure constant pressure at 
the flow regulating needle valves. It is necessary to pass the carbon dioxide 
through a heat exchanger installed ahead of the regulating valves to 
prevent freezing of the valves. The gases are passed through a metering 
system consisting of two calibrated rotameter flow meters, to indicate the 
proportion of the two gases mixed in the surge tank. Any number of lamp 
assemblies may be operated as a unit, the throughput of the flow meters 
being chosen accordingly. The tubing that connects that chimney 
manifold to the chimneys should have an internal diameter not smaller 
than 6*4 mm in order to prevent unnecessary restriction in gas flow. The 
scrubber should have a capacity of about 1 litre. 

3.4.1 The vacuum manifold shall be connected to a pump of sufficient 
capacity to permit a steady gas flow of about 3 litres per minute through 
each absorber and to maintain a constant manifold pressure of approxi- 
mately 40 mbar below atmospheric. The gas mixture in the chimney 
manifold shall be maintained at nearly constant pressure of 1 to 2 mbar 
and the burner manifold at approximately 20 mbar. Any other system 
similar to the one described here may also be used. Modifications of the 
manifold and associated equipment for burning samples in air are shown 
in Fig. 6 and described in Method B. 

4. REAGENTS AND MATERIALS 

4.1 Carbon Dioxide and Oxygen — The carbon dioxide and oxygen 
shall each be at least 99*5 percent pure, meeting the requirements prescri- 
bed in 7.1.5. 

4.2 Diluent — The diluent used shall have a sulphur content less than 
001 percent, completely miscible with the sample J to be analyzed and 
permit burning at a moderate rate without smoking. n-Heptane, wo-octane 
and absolute ethyl alcohol have been found suitable. 

4.3 Dilate Hydrochloric Acid ( 1 : 10 ) — Mix 1 volume of concentrated 
hydrochloric acid ( see IS : 265-1976* ) with 10 volumes of water. 

4.4 Hydrogen Peroxide ( 1 : 19 ) — Mix 1 volume of hydrogen peroxide 
( 30 percent ) with 19 volumes of water. Store in a dark coloured glass- 
stoppered bottle. 

4.5 Methyl Purple Indicator — Aqueous solution containing approxi- 
mately 0*1 percent active constituent ( do not use methyl violet).

4.6 Sodium Hydroxide Solution ( 10 Percent ) — Dissolve 100 g of 
technical grade sodium hydroxide pellets in water and dilute to 1 litre. 

4.7 Sodium Hydroxide, Standard Solution ( 0-05 N ) — Dilute 2'8 ml 
of saturated sodium hydroxide solution to 1 litre ( see Note ), using for this 
purpose the clear saturated solution decanted after standing long enough 
to permit any precipitate to settle out. The solution should be standardi- 
zed by titration against standard acid, using methyl purple indicator. 
Store in an alkali-resistant glass bottle and protect to minimize contamina- 
tion by CO) from the air. Use only pure gum rubber tubing for connec- 
tions between the storage bottles and burettes. 

Note — The calculation of results may be simplified by adjusting the normality 
of the sodium hydroxide solution to 0*062 4 ± 0*000 1 . Then 1 ml of sodium 
hydroxide solution will be equivalent to 0*001 g of sulphur. In this case, the factor 
lb'03 N in the calculation ( see 7.4.1 ) becomes 1000. 

5. PREPARATION OF APPARATUS 

5.1 When the apparatus is first assembled, charge the absorber with 
30 ± 2 ml of water. Adjust the individual valves between the vacuum 
manifold and spray traps so that approximately 3 litres of air per minute 
will be drawn through each absorber when the chimney outlets are open 
to the atmosphere, while maintaining the pressure in the vacuum manifold 
at approximately 40 mbar ( cm ) of water below atmospheric. When all 
adjustments have been made, remove the water from the absorbers. The 
height of the liquids in the pressure and vacuum regulators is indicated in 
Fig. 5 and during operation a slow leak of gas through them should be 
maintained. 

Note— In use, place 300 to 400 ml, of hydrogen peroxide ( V5 percent ) in the 
scrubber. Since the manifold manometer also serves as a scrubber at the end of the 
test to remove carbon dioxide from the absorbent, use hydrogen peroxide as the 
manometric liquid. Replace weekly or whenever the volume becomes appreciably 
less than the original. 

5.2 Neutralize the hydrogen peroxide ( 1 : 19 ) immediately before use. 
As 30 ml of the solution is needed, transfer to a beaker multiples of 30 ml 
sufficient for the number of absorbers to be used simultaneously. Add 
1 drop of methyl purple indicator solution for each 100 ml of hydrogen 
peroxide and then add standard sodium hydroxide solution drop-wise 
until the colour changes from purple to light green. 

5.3 Introduce 30 ± 2 ml of the freshly neutralized hydrogen peroxide 
( 1 : 19) into the larger bulb of each absorber. In addition, for each set 
of samples burned, prepare an extra absorber for use as a control blank. 
Attach the spray traps and chimneys and connect them to their respective 
manifolds by means of sulphur-free rubber tubing. Close the chimney 
openings by means of corks. 



IS : 1448 [ P : 34 ] - 1979 

5.4 With burner control valves closed, the valve to the vacuum regulator 
fully open, and the pressure in the vacuum manifold adjusted to approxi- 
mately 40 mbar ( cm ) of water below atmospheric, turn on the carbon 
dioxide and oxygen supplies (CAUTION — see Note 1). Adjust the 
chimney manifold control valve so that, at the required rate of flow 
through the absorbers, only a small stream of carbon dioxide-oxygen 
escapes at the pressure regulator, a small stream of air enters at the vacuum 
regulator, and the pressure in the chimney manifold is 1 to 2 mbar ( cm ) 
of water. Minor adjustment of the vacuum regulator and vacuum control 
valve may be necessary to achieve this condition ( see Note 2 ). 

Notk 1 — CAUTION : A hazardous ( explosive ) condition may result if the 
carbon dioxide supply is interrupted and the oxygen flow is continued while 
samples are being burned. The installation of suitable warning or control equipment 
is recommended. 

Notk 2 — It is convenient to balance the gas flow system by regulating the 
pressure in the vacuum manifold. This is done by raising or lowering the air inlet 
tube in the vacuum regulator by sliding it in a rubber sleeve. 

5.5 Cut the wicking to 30 cm lengths. Use the number of lengths dictated 
by the sample (see 6) and fold the wicking once to give a 15 cm long 
bundle for threading the burners. Thread the required number of burners 
by inserting the looped ends into the top of the inner tube of the burner. 
Draw the wicking through by means of a metal hojk. Trim the wick as 
close as possible to the top of the burner with a pair of sharp scissors. It 
is essential that thoroughly cleaned burners and new wicking be used for 
each test. 

6. CONTROL OF COMBUSTION 

6.1 Most types of liquid samples burn with a luminous yellow flame, the 
size and shape of which is dependent on the gas flow to the burner, the 
volatility of the material, the tightness of the fit of the wick in the burner 
tube, and the position of the top of the wick relative to the top of the 
burner. It is preferable that the latter two variables be fixed with relation 
to the first before burning is started so that the flame may be controlled 
by variation in the rate of carbon dioxide-oxygen flow. 

6.2 Highly volatile samples require a tight-fitting wick, the top of which 
may need to be several millimetres below the top of the burner, and in 
extreme cases may have to be cooled in ice during the burning. Less 
volatile materials require a more loosely fitting wick and may require 
warming. 

6.3 After trimming, draw the wick down until the trimmed edge is flush 
with or just a little below the top of the burner. With the burner for 
aromatic samples, the distance from the top of the burner to the top of the 
wicking should be 8 mm or more for benzene and 4 mm for toluene; slight 
heating of the upper end of the burner will be helpful in starting vapo- 
rization of heavier materials. 

10 



IS : 1448 [P : 34 ]-1979 

6.4 To use the standard lamp, light the wick and then slowly admit 
combustion atmosphere to the burner to obtain a smoke-free flame. To 
use the burner for aromatic samples, introduce a small amount of combus- 
tion atmosphere into the flask to provide sufficient vapour for lighting the 
burner. After lighting the burner, introduce combustion atmosphere 
directly into the burner to prevent smoking and to adjust the flame size. 
If the flame is accidentally snuffed out, relight. 

6.5 A short burning period ( 1 to 2 minutes are usually sufficient ) at low 
flame height is necessary to allow combustion to reach equilibrium before 
the flame size may be increased without causing a smoky flame. In adjust- 
ing the standard lamp, the entire control is at the burner. For the burner 
for aromatic samples, first adjust the flow of gas to the flask and then 
reduce the flow of gas to the burner as required. In any case, it is essential 
that the flame burns smoothly and symmetrically and without jets in the 
inner cone or smoke on the outer fringes. 

6.6 Satisfactory combustion of materials difficult to burn may sometimes 
be obtained by increasing the oxygen content of the combustion atmos- 
phere. Never increase the oxygen content of the combustion atmosphere 
to more than 40 percent. 

6.7 Before extinguishing the flame, the samples shall be burned until the 
flask and wicking appear to be dry and the flame has reduced consider- 
ably in size; frequently the flame continues to burn a short time after the 
flask appears dry because of the sample in the wick. For example, for 
gasoline samples, which burn with a high flame, the flame should be 
extinguished when it is only 3 to 4 mm high. If the flame is permitted to 
burn until it goes out, partially oxidized substances ( probably organic 
acids ) are produced; as a result, broad and indistinct end points are 
obtained. When samples are not burned until the flask is apparently dry, 
erratic results may be obtained. In the case of volatile samples, any 
unburned sample will escape from the burner during weighing. When 
elemental sulphur is present, it is particularly important that the sample 
be burned to apparent dryness and that the wick be maintained flush with 
the top of the burner to ensure complete combustion. With mixtures 
containing light and heavy hydrocarbons, the more volatile materials 
seem to burn first, possibly concentrating sulphur compounds in the 
material remaining behind. 

7. METHOD A 

7.1 Procedure for Direct Combustion of Liquid Samples 

7.1.1 Introduce into the flask of each lamp an approximate quantity of 
sample by means of an appropriate pipette, as indicated in Table l f 

11 



18 : 1448 [ P : 34 ] . 1979 

Stopper the flasks with clean, numbered corks. Weigh each flask and its 
burner to the nearest 0*005 g. 

Note -—While the stoppered flasks and prepared burners may all be weighed 
separately, it is usually more convenient to place each flask and its burner on the 
balance pan and obtain the combined mass in single weighing.

7*1*2 Handling each lamp individually, insert the burner in the flask. 
As soon as the sample has risen by capillary action to the top of the wick, 
connect the side tube of the burner to the burner manifold by means of 
sulphur-free rubber tubing. Light the burner with a sulphur-free flame 
( such as an alcohol lamp ) and insert into the chimney, pinching off the 
connection between the chimney and the chimney manifold during the 
insertion if the flame tends to be blown out. At the same time, adjust the 
gas flow to the burner so that the flame is maintained at a point just below 
smoking and has a steady symmetrical appearance. Continue in this 
manner until all lamps have been placed in the chimneys. Make any 
minor adjustment of the chimney manifold control valve necessary to 
maintain the required pressure (see 5). During the burning, and parti- 
cularly during the later stages when the flame becomes small, decrease the 
carbon dioxide-oxygen supply to the burners in order to prevent extinction 
of the flame ( see Note ). 

Note — When incomplete combustion occurs, the absorber liquid will foam 
excessively. 

7.1.3 When the burning of each sample is complete, as evidenced by 
the flame becoming small due to depletion of the sample, remove the 
burner and flask from the chimney, extinguish the flame, shut off the 
carbon dioxide-oxygen supply to the burner, and stopper the chimney 
opening. Immediately reweigh the flask, burner and numbered cork. 
When all combustions have been completed, turn off the carbon dioxide 
and the oxygen supplies, close the chimney control valve and close the 
connection to the vacuum regulator. This will cause air to be drawn into 
the chimney manifold through the manometer. Allow air to be drawn 

1? 



IS : 1441 [ P : 34 ] . 1971 

through the absorbers in this manner for 5 minutes to remove dissolved 
carbon dioxide from the absorbent, then close the vacuum control valve. 

Note — If it is desired to conserve the combustion atmosphere, the gas flow 
through each individual absorber may be turned off upon completion of the burning 
period. To accomplish this, pinch off the rubber tubing connecting the spray trap to the 
vacuum manifold, reduce the flow of mixed gases at the rotameters proportionately, 
and readjust the vacuum control valve and the chimney control valve. When the 
burning of all samples has been completed, it is necessary to remove the pinch 
clamps and readjust the vacuum control valve in order to draw air at the required 
rate through the absorbers for removal of dissolved carbon dioxide. 

7*1*4 Rinse the chimneys and spray traps three times, using about 
10 ml of water each time. When the sample contains lead anti-knock 
fluids, use hot water to rinse the chimneys. Add the rinsings to the 
absorbers and titrate as directed in 7.3. 

7.1.5 Blank — Leave the chimney of the blank absorber ( see 5.3 ) 
stoppered and allow the carbon dioxide-oxygen stream to pass through 
that absorber until all samples started at one time have finished burning. 
Turn off the carbon dioxide and oxygen supplies and aerate the blank 
absorber in the same manner as sample absorbers ( see 7.1.3 ). Titrate the 
absorber liquid as directed in 7.3. Normally, the combustion blank will 
be small, but if the titration requires more than 0*1 ml of standard sodium 
hydroxide solution, discard the determination and replace the carbon 
dioxide cylinder. 

7.2 Procedure for Blending and Combustion of Liquid Samples 

7.2.1 Add 6 ml of sulphur-free diluent to each flask. Stopper the flasks 
with numbered corks and weigh to the nearest 0*005 g. By means of a 
pipette introduce into the flask of each burner an approximate quantity 
of sample as indicated in Table 2; swirl to mix thoroughly and reweigh. 
Alternatively, make a quantitative 40 percent blend of the sample in 
sulphur-free diluent and proceed as described in 7.1. 

TABLE 2 SAMPLE SIZE FOR TESTING BLENDED LIQUID SAMPLES 

Sulphur Content, 
Percent by Mass 

0*5 and under 
Over 0*5 

7.2.2 Insert the burner and burn as described in 7.1.2. Remove each 
lamp from its chimney as the flame nears extinction and extinguish the 
flame. Add 2 ml of diluent to rinse down the walls of the flask. Burn 
the additional diluent and repeat the addition of diluent and burning so 
that a total of 10 ml of diluent has been burned,

Note— It is desirable that 10 ml diluent blank be run; the titration of the 
absorber solution from this blank should not exceed 0*1 ml of standard sodium 
hydroxide solution. 

7.2.3 After all lamps have completed burning, turn off the carbon 
dioxide and oxygen supplies, close the connection to the vacuum regulator, 
draw air through the absorbers for 5 minutes and finally close the vacuum 
control valve. Rinse the chimneys and spray traps three times, using 
about 10 ml of water each time. Add the rinsings to the absorbers and 
titrate as directed in 7.3. 

7.3 Titration of Absorbent Solution — Add 3 to 4 drops of methyl 
purple indicator solution to the liquid in each absorber. Titrate the 
absorbent solution by introducing 005 N sodium hydroxide solution from 
a burette into the smaller bulb of the absorber. Use a 10 ml micro-burette 
if less than 10 mg of sulphur is expected to be present in the absorber. 
Stir during the titration by applying suction intermittently to the top of 
the larger bulb. 

Notb — When incomplete combustion of the sample occurs, the air drawn 
through the absorber during the titration will have a characteristic taste or odour and 
the end point will be broad. In these cases, discard the determination. 

7.4 Calculation 

7.4.1 Calculate the sulphur content of liquid samples as follows:

7.4.2 When it is required to correct the sulphur content ( see Note ) for 
lead antiknock fluids, calculate the corrected values as follows: 

Corrected sulphur content, percent by mass = S — 3785 Z LF 

where 

S «= sulphur content, percent by mass; 

L «= lead content in g per litre; and 

F= 001 5 if the sample contains aviation lead anti-knock fluid 
or 0-003 5 if the sample contains tetraethyl lead, tetramethyl 
lead, or the mixed lead alkyl anti-knock fluid.

Note — These corrections are based on experiments of burning fuels blended 
with anti-knock fluid containing tetraethyl lead and ethylene halide in commonly 
used combinations. Tetramethyl lead and the mixed lead alkyl anti-knock fluids 
contain the same ethylene halide combination as the tetraethyl had fluid, 

7.5 Report — Report the result of the test to the nearest 0*01 percent 
for sulphur at a level of 005 percent and higher. 

7.6 Precision — Results of duplicate tests shall not differ by more than 
the following amounts:

where

8. METHOD B ( AIR BURNING OF SAMPLE — GRAVIMETRIC 
FINISH ) 

8.0 Scope and Field of Application — This procedure is recommended 
only for analyzing liquid petroleum samples that can be burned with a 
wick lamp; it is not recommended for analysis of liquefied petroleum gas 
samples. 

8.1 Apparatus — The manifold system described in 3.4 may be used with 
only a slight modification. Substitute filtered air for the carbon dioxide- 
oxygen supply train and add a second sintered-plate scrubber to the 
incoming air-line as shown in Fig. 6. 

8.2 Reagents — In addition to the reagents given in 4, the following 
reagents are required. 

8.2.1 Barium Chloride Solution ( 10 Percent ) — Dissolve 100 g of barium 
chloride dihydrate ( BaCl r 2H 2 ) in water and dilute to 1 litre. 

8.2.2 Concentrated Hydrochloric Acid — See IS : 265-1976*. 

8.2.3 Concentrated Hydrogen Peroxide — 30 percent. 

8.2.4 Dilute Sulphuric Acid {1:16) — Mix 60 ml of concentrated 
sulphuric acid ( see IS : 266-1977t ) with 960 ml of water. 

8.3 Preparation of Apparatus 

8.3.1 Place 300 to 400 ml of sodium hydroxide solution {see AS) in the 
first scrubber ( Fig. 6 ) and the same amount of a solution prepared by 



♦Specification for hydrochloric acid ( second revision ). 
fSpecification for sulphuric acid ( second revision ).

mixing 300 ml of water, 30 ml of dilute sulphuric acid and 30 ml of 
concentrated hydrogen peroxide in the second scrubber. For apparatus 
in daily use, replace these solutions two times each week or whenever the 
volume becomes less than two thirds of the original. 

8.3.2 Make other preparations as in 5, except that the hydrogen 
peroxide (1 : 19 ) need not be neutralized, 

8.4 Procedure for Combustion — Use a sample size as prescribed in 
Table 3. Burn the sample as in 7.1 controlling combustion as in 6. 
Analyze the absorber solution from the samples and blank as described 
in 8.5.

8.5 Procedure for Analysis of Absorber Solution 

8.5.1 Transfer the absoiber liquid to a 400-ml beaker. Rinse the 
absorber and chimney thoroughly with water and add the rinsings to the 
beaker. Filter the solution to remove any foreign material, receiving the 
filtrate in a 400-ml beaker having* a mark to indicate 75 ml. Add 2 ml 
of concentrated hydrochloric acid, heat to boiling, and add 10 ml of 
barium chloride solution, either in a fine stream or dropwise. Stir the 
solution during the addition and for 2 minutes thereafter. 

8.5*2 Cover the beaker with a fluted watch-glass and continue boiling 
slowly until the solution has evaporated to a volume of approximately 
75 ml, as indicated by the mark on the beaker. Remove the beaker from 
the source of heat and allow to cool for one hour before filtering. 

8.5.3 Filter the supernatant liquid through a close-texture, ashless filter 
paper. Wash the precipitate wilh water, first by decantation and then on 
the filter paper, until free of chloride ion. Transfer the paper and 
precipitate to a suitable weighed crucible, and dry at low heat until the 
moisture has evaporated. Char the paper completely without igniting it, 
and finally ignite at a bright red heat until the precipitate is burned white 
( set Note ). After ignition is complete, allow the crucible to cool to room 
temperature and weigh. 

Note — A satisfactory means of accomplishing these operations is to place the 
uncovered crucible containing the wet filter paper in a cold electric muffle furnace 
and turn on the current. Drying, charring, and ignition usually occur at the desired 
rate.

Note — The determination should be discarded if the blank correction used in 
the calculation exceeds 1*5 mg of barium sulphate. Frequently, impure reagents 
are the cause of this difficulty. 

8.7 Report — Report the result as in 7.5. 

8.8 Precision — - The precision values are the same as given in 7.6. 

9. METHOD C ( METHOD OF TEST FOR TRACE QUANTITIES 
OF SULPHUR ) 

9.0 Scope and Field of Application — This method extends the lamp 
method of test for sulphur to the analysis of samples having sulphur 
contents as low as 5 ppm ( see Note ). The procedure is not applicable for 
the determination of less than 300 ppm of sulphur in liquids containing 
lead anti-knock compounds. 

Note — Only by exercise of the most scrupulous care and attention to details 
may reliable results be obtained by this method. Before placing new glassware into 
use and thereafter as required, wash the glassware with concentrated nitric acid. 
Rinse three times with tap water, followed by three rinsings with de-ionized distilled 
water. Reserve units of glassware for use in this method alone. 

9.1 Outline of the Method — A test portion of suitable size is burned as 
described in the Method A. Sulphate ion in the absorbed solution is 
determined by precipitation as barium sulphate, and turbidity of a 
suspension of the precipitate, stabilized by the addition of ethanol and 
glycerine, is measured by using a spectrophotometer or filter photometer. 

9.2 Apparatus — In addition to the apparatus given in 3, the following 
apparatus is required. 

9.2.1 Photometer — preferably a spectrophotometer having an effective 
band width of about 50 nm and equipped with a blue-sensitive phototube 
for use at 450 nm or alternatively a filter photometer equipped with a 
colour filter having a maximum transmission at approximately 425 nm. 

IS 



IS : 1448 [ P : 34 ] - 19W 

9.2*2 Absorption Cells — cells having optical path lengths of 50 mm are 
preferred. With use, the cells may become coated with a film. To remove 
this film, wash the cells with a detergent using a soft brush. Rinse 
thoroughly with de-ionized water following cleaning. 

Note — The procedure as given assumes an absorbance change of about 0*100 
for each 0*1 mg or sulphur in 50 ml of solution measured in a 50 mm cell. Photo- 
meters employing cells of shorter optical paths give proportionately poorer precision. 

9.2.3 Scoop — capable of dispensing 0*30 ± 0*01 g of barium chloride 
dihydrate crystals ( 500 to 850 (zm size ). 

9.2.4 Magnetic Stirrer — equipped with polytctrafluoroethylene covered 
stirring bar about 30 mm long. 

9.2.5 Lamp Assembly — as described in 3. Reserve complete units con- 
sisting of flask, burner, chimney, absorber, and spray trap for use in this 
procedure only. 

9.3 Reagents — In addition to the reagents prescribed in 4, the following 
reagents are required. 

9.3.1 Alcohol-Glycerine Mixture — Mix 2 volumes of ethyl alcohol 
(95 percent v\v) with one volume of glycerine. 

9.3.2 Barium Chloride Dihydrate ( BaCl t .2H^0 ) — 500 to 850 (xm size 
crystals. 

Note — The crystal size of the barium chloride dihydrate is an important 
variable that affects the development of turbidity. 

9.3.3 Hydrochloric Acid {1:12) — Add 77 ml of concentrated hydro- 
chloric acid ( see IS : 265-1976*) to a 1-litre volumetric flask and dilute 
to the mark with de-ionized water. 

9.3.4 Dilute Hydrochloric Acid (1 : 215)— Add 60 ml of hydrochloric 
acid as prepared in 9.3.3 to a litre volumetric flask and dilute to the mark 
with de-ionized water. 

9.3.5 Standard Sulphuric Acid ( 1 ml «= 0*100 mgS)— Dilute 6*24 ± 001 
ml of sulphuric acid ( 1 N ) to exactly 1 litre with de-ionized water. Check 
the dilution by titration against standard sodium hydroxide solution of 
about the same normality and adjust the concentration, if necessary, so 
that each millilitre of this solution is equivalent to 0*100 mg of sulphur (S). 

9.3.6 Water 9 De-ionized — Percolate distilled water through a column of 
mixed anion and cation exchange resins. 

Note — A means for determining when to replace the exchange resins should 
be supplied. Use of a simple electrical conductivity meter has been found satis- 
factory for this purpose. 



♦ Specification for hydrochloric acid ( second revision ). 

19 



IS : 1448 [f>: 34] -1979 

9.4 Calibration 

9.4.1 Into a series of eight 50-ml volumetric flasks, introduce, by meant 
of a burette, 025, 050, 0*75, 100, 1*50, 200, 300 and 500 ml of sulphuric 
acid ( 1 ml = 0100 mg S ). Add 30 ml of hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 12 ) to 
each flask, dilute to volume with water and mix thoroughly. Prepare a 
reagent blank in a similar way, omitting the sulphuric acid. 

9.4.2 Pour the entire contents of each flask into a 100 ml beaker, add 
by means of a pipette 10*0 ±0*1 ml of alcohol-glycerine mixture, and mix 
for 3 minutes on the magnetic stirrer. Select a stirring speed just below 
that which might cause splashing. Maintain this speed throughout the 
entire procedure. 

9.4.3 Allow the solution to stand undisturbed for 4 minutes. Transfer to 
an absorption cell and measure the initial absorbance, using water as 
reference. 

9.4.4 Return the solution to the beaker and add 0*30 ±0*01 g of 
barium chloride dihydrate crystals, either by weighing this amount or by 
use of the scoop. Stir with the magnetic stirrer for exactly 3 minutes. Allow 
to stand for an additional 4 minutes, transfer to the cell, and again 
measure the absorbance relative to water. 

9.4.5 Following steps described in 9.4.2 to 9.4.4, obtain a reagent blank 
reading by subtracting the initial absorbance of the reagent blank from 
that obtained after addition of barium chloride dihydrate. This reading 
should not exceed 005. 

9.4.6 Obtain the net absorbance for each standard by subtracting the 
initial absorbance and reagent blank reading from the absorbance 
obtained in accordance with 9.4.4. Plot the net absorbance of each 
standard against milligrams of sulphur contained in 50 ml of solution, and 
draw a smooth curve through the points. 

9.4.7 Check the calibration curve daily by making single determina- 
tions to detect possible shifts. 

9.5 Procedure for Combustion of Samples 

9.5.1 Prepare the combustion apparatus and burn between 5 to 30 g of 
sample depending on the expected sulphur level ( see Note ). Follow the 
general procedures described in 5, 6 and 7.1 or 10. The requirements for 
initial neutralization of the hydrogen peroxide ( see 5.2 ) and for final 
removal of dissolved carbon dioxide from this solution ( see 7.1.3, 7.2.3 
and 10.1.7 ) may be omitted. Draw combustion atmosphere through one 
absorber of a set to serve as a blank on the purity of this atmosphere. 
Reserve all glassware exclusively for use with this trace procedure to avoid 

20 



IS:1448[P:34]-1979 

any possible contamination from other sources. Transfer the absorber 
solution, containing rinsings from the spray trap and chimney ( see 7.1.4 
and 10.1.7 ), to a 250-ml beaker, rinse the absorber two or three times 
with 10-ml portions of water and add the rinsings to the solution in the 
beaker. 

Note — A sample size that will yield between 0*15 and 2*5 mg of sulphur in 
the absorber, shall be selected. This will then allow subsequent direct application 
of the procedures described in 9.5,3 and 9.6 and will avoid the necessity for using 
less than a one-fifth aliquot of the absorber solution for analysis. When the sulphur 
level of the sample is about 15 ppm or less, at least 30 g of sample shall be burned. 
To accommodate the large sample sizes, a burner flask of suitable size shall be 
fabricated to replace the standard 25 ml flask. In recognition of the larger size of 
the flask, it is preferable to use 180 mm of wicking rather than the 150 mm specified 
in 5.5. To avoid excessive depletion of absorber liquid caused by the longer burning 
time for larger samples, it is preferable to charge the absorbers with 50 ± 3 ml of 
the hydrogen peroxide instead of 30 ± 2 ml specified in 5.3. 

9.5.2 Reduce the volume of the absorber solution to about 20 ml by 
evaporation on a hot-plate. Quantitatively transfer the resulting solution 
to a 50-ml volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker with several small portions 
of water. Add 3 ml of hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 12 ) to the flask, make up to 
volume with water, and mix thoroughly. 

9.5.3 If the sulphur content of the absorber solution is known to be less 
than 0*5 mg, use the entire contents of the volumetric flask for analysis. If 
the approximate sulphur content is unknown or is expected to exceed 0*5 
mg, transfer a 10 ml aliquot to a second 50 ml volumetric flask and dilute 
to solution in both flasks to volume with dilute hydrochloric acid ( 1 : 215 ). 
Use the more dilute solution first and, if less than 0*50 mg of sulphur is 
found, then use the more concentrated solution. Prepare a dilution of the 
combustion atmosphere blank similar to the solution used for analysis. 
Analyze the solution as described in 9.6. 

9.6 Procedure for Analysis of Solutions 

9.6.1 Pour the entire contents of the 50-ml volumetric flask containing 
the solution to be analyzed into a 100 ml beaker and proceed as directed 
in 9.4.2, 9.4.3 and 9.4.4. Treat the combustion atmosphere blank in the 
same way and obtain a combustion atmosphere-reagent blank reading by 
subtracting its initial absorbance from that obtained after addition of 
barium chloride dihydrate crystals. 

Note — If the blank reading exceeds 0020, the precision obtainable will be 
impaired. In this event, make an analysis of the reagents alone to determine 
whether the atmosphere or reagents are at fault. Place 30 ml of hydrogen peroxide 
( 1*5 percent ) in the 50-ml volumetric flask, dilute to the mark with dilute hydro- 
chloric acid ( 1 :215), and proceed as described in 9.4.5. If this reagent blank 
reading exceeds 0010, results should not be considered reliable. 

21 



IS : 1448 I P : 34 ] - 1979 

9.6.2 Obtain the net absorbance of the analysis solution by subtract- 
ing the initial absorbance and the combustion atmosphere-reagent blank 
reading from that obtained after addition of barium chloride dihydrate 
crystals. 

9.6.3 Convert net absorbance to milligrams of sulphur by using the 
calibration curve. 

9.7 Calculation — Calculate the amount of sulphur in the sample as 
follows:

where 



A a sulphur content in mg of the analysis solution read from 
the calibration curve; 

W =3 grams of sample burned; and 

F «= aliquot fraction of absorber solution used for analysis.

10. METHOD D ( LIQUEFIED PETROLEUM GASES ) 

10.1 Procedure 

10*1.1 Obtain the sample as prescribed in 1447-1966*. 

10.1.2 Clean and dry a 100 ml corrosion-resistant metal vessel. 
Remove the needle valve. Wash the interior of the vessel and needle 
valve, first with a sulphur-free hydrocarbon, such as n-pentane, and then 
with acetone. Dry the interior of the vessel with clean, compressed air, 
and rinse it with hydrochloric acid ( I : 10). Rinse the interior with 
water and then rinse it with sodium hydroxide solution ( 100 g per litre ). 
Rinse the interior of the vessel with water until the wash-water is neutral 



•Mcthodi of sampling of petroleum and its products. 

22 



IS:1448[P:34Mft76 

to a ^H test paper. Wash the vessel with acetone, and allow it to drain 
for at least 10 minutes. Dry the vessel with a stream of clean, comp- 
ressed air, and reassemble. 

10-1.3 Evacuate the clean, dried metal vessel, and connect it to the 
liquid line of the sample container by means of a short length of stainless 
steel tubing, leaving the connection to the metal vessel somewhat loose. 
Open the valve slightly on the sample container and allow a small amount 
of the sample to bleed from the loose connection at the metal vessel, 
thereby purging the transfer line ( CAUTION — see Note ). Take care to 
exclude all air when filling the metal vessel because hydrogen sulphide 
oxidizes rapidly in the presence of metals. Tighten the connection at the 
metal vessel and introduce 30 to 50 g of the liquid phase of the sample 
into the evacuated metal vessel. 

Note — CAUTION: If this sample transfer is made in a building, observe all 
necessary fire precautions. 

10.1.4 Immediately, disconnect the metal vessel and bleed off the 
liquid phase of the sample until the net mass in the 100 ml metal vessel is 
30 to 40 g. 

Note — CAUTION: It is important not to keep the sample vessel liquid full 
because further liquid expansion on increase of temperature could rupture the 
vessel. 

10.1.5 Weigh the vessel containing the sample to the nearest 1 g. 
Support the sample vessel in an inverted position so that the sample is 
taken from the liquid phase. Connect the sample vessel to the auxiliary 
stainless steel regulating valve by means of stainless steel tubing ( see 
Fig. 7 ). By means of short lengths of sulphur-free rubber tubing, connect 
the auxiliary valve outlet to the side inlet of the gas burner and the lower 
inlet of the gas burner to the burner manifold. 

Note — With some samples it may become necessary, for steady burning, to 
surround the auxiliary valve with a heat-exchanger system. A convenient means is 
winding insulated heating wire, having a resistance of 40 to 60 ohms, around the 
auxiliary valve and connecting it to a suitable rheostat. Another means is to place 
the regulating valve in a suitable metal beaker and cover the valve body with water 
maintained at 60 to 80°C. 

10.1.6 Open the valve on the sample vessel; then open the auxiliary 
valve to allow a small stream of vapour to escape. Quickly light the 
burner with a sulphur-free flame. Adjust the flow of carbon dioxide- 
oxygen mixture and sample so that the flame is approximately 35 mm high 
and clear blue in colour; this colour is reached just beyond the point at 
which a yellow colour shows at the tip of the flame. Insert the burner into 
the chimney and re-adjust the flame if necessary. Burn approximately the 
quantity of sample prescribed in Table 4. Close the valve on the sample 
vessel and allow the sample contained between this valve and the auxiliary 
valve to be vapourized and burned. Disconnect the heated auxiliary valve 
and reweigh the sample vessel to the nearest 0*1 g.

10.1.7 When the combustions have been completed, turn off the carbon 
dioxide and oxygen supplies, remove the burner from the chimney, close 
the valve to the vacuum regulator, draw air through the absorbeis for 
5 minutes, and finally close the vacuum control valve. Rinse the chimneys 
and spray traps three times, using about 10 ml of water each time. Add 
the rinsings to the absorbers and titrate as directed in 7.3.

10.3 Report — Report the result as in 7.5.
